meta.title: Yoruba B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1000 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Yoruba → English (see the Yoruba, recall the meaning) and English → Yoruba (see an English meaning, recall the Yoruba). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1000 words for an intermediate learner, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise while travelling, to produce simple connected text on familiar topics, and to describe experiences and events, dreams, hopes and ambitions, and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. AT THIS LEVEL THE SOURCES RUN THIN: English Wiktionary lacks much of what a B1 topic list would hold (government, law, health), so the written part was chosen from the everyday words Wiktionary does have, and the last words dealt by frequency appear in only one or two articles, so their order says little. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Yoruba, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 141 of the 1000 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — time and how often, family and people, work and trades, school and knowledge, machines and the media, the home and the kitchen, food and drink, the body and health, animals and the wild, travel and the world, society and rights, and the verbs of doing and thinking — and the other 859 are the commonest remaining words of the Yoruba Wikipedia (its articles of 150 words or more, the one-line stubs left out). About half of that Wikipedia is written with its tone marks, and the counts of the carefully marked articles decide how an unmarked spelling is shared out among the words it could be (ti, tí, tì). The corpus is encyclopaedic, which shows in the fill (government, history, sport), and the cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words met most often come first. Only words English Wiktionary has an entry for can be taught here, and some of the commonest are missing from it (ta ni 'who', ibo 'where', nísinsìnyí 'now', tún 'again', burú 'to be bad'). Every word is written in standard Yoruba spelling WITH ITS TONE MARKS — an acute for a high tone (á), a grave for a low one (à), no mark for a mid tone — because the tones are part of the word: ọkọ is 'husband', ọkọ̀ 'vehicle', ọkọ́ 'hoe'. The Alphabet deck, first in this collection, teaches the letters and the marks. One spelling is often several words (dá 'to create', 'to stop', 'to break'); the card is the spelling and gives the first meaning of each. Many Yoruba adjectives are verbs ('to be big', 'to be good'), and are taught as Wiktionary gives them. Example sentences are few: 170 of the 1000 words have one, from Wiktionary's usage examples and from Tatoeba, which holds about 60 Yoruba sentences with a translation; none is invented. There is no speaker button: few devices have a Yoruba voice, and one without it would read the word in another language's sounds. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, spellings and tone marks: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Yoruba Wikipedia, articles of the 2026-11-01 dump (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: English Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
